newsitem.title: CHINA: Britain Labour deputy talks Hong Kong in China.
newsitem.headline: Britain Labour deputy talks Hong Kong in China.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party, favourite to win power in the next few months, is hoping for a smooth transition when Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule in June, party deputy leader John Prescott said on Friday.

Labour was united with Britain's ruling Conservatives in opposing Beijing's plans to scrap Hong Kong's existing elected legislature when it regains control of the British colony on July 1, 1997, Prescott told reporters in the Chinese capital.

Hong Kong had been a major topic in meetings with senior Chinese leaders, including economic tsar Zhu Rongji, and Labour was eager to improve its contacts with Beijing before the handover at midnight on June 30, he said.
"The whole world will be looking at this transition," Prescott said.

"We want it to go well whether it is under a Tory (Conservative) government or a Labour government. Updating ourselves and improving contacts with different people in the government in China is important, and I think we have achieved that," he said.

Labour is widely expected to win Britain's next general election, which must be held by May 22 at the latest, making the the potentially stormy Hong Kong handover a possible foreign policy headache for a new Labour adminstration.

Prescott said Labour was not trying to negotiate separately with the Chinese government, which has clashed frequently with London over handover issues ranging from construction contracts to the future of the elected legislature.

However, he said Labour disagreed with the Conservatives in believing that Britain should be more ready to grant residence rights to thousands of non-ethnic Chinese Hong Kong residents whose post-transition status was still unclear.

The party was trying to look beyond the handover period, said Prescott, who was scheduled to visit China's southern Guangdong province with a trade delegation from his home constituency before travelling to Hong Kong.
"We are looking to the opportunity to look forward...from the transition," he said. "That isn't the end of the contract of Britain with China."
